title: Fundoscopy in Clinical Medicine
subject: Medicine
summary: Fundoscopy is a bedside eye examination that reveals systemic disease. It helps grade hypertensive, diabetic and infectious retinopathies, and detects raised intracranial pressure. In low‑resource settings, it guides urgent management when labs are unavailable.

sections.p: Fundoscopy is the direct visualisation of the retina, optic disc, macula and retinal vessels using an ophthalmoscope. It is performed with the patient sitting upright, focusing on a distant point, and the examiner looking through the pupil.
b: Provides a window to systemic microvascular health
Can be done with a simple handheld ophthalmoscope, no dilating drops required for a quick screen

sections.p: Retinopathies are staged by recognised grading systems that correlate with systemic risk.
b: Hypertensive retinopathy: Keith–Wagener–Barker grades I‑IV (grade IV = papilloedema)
Diabetic retinopathy: Mild, moderate non‑proliferative, severe non‑proliferative, proliferative
Papilloedema: Graded by Frisén scale (1‑5) if photography available

sections.p: Identify the most common aetiologies in East African and other low‑resource hospitals.
b: Hypertensive emergency/malignant hypertension
Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
Severe malaria with retinal haemorrhages
HIV‑related CMV retinitis or opportunistic infections
Tuberculosis meningitis causing papilloedema
Sickle cell disease with proliferative retinopathy

sections.p: Patients may present with visual symptoms or systemic signs that prompt a retinal look.
b: Sudden visual loss, floaters, or scotomas
Headache, vomiting, or altered consciousness suggesting raised ICP
Systemic hypertension, proteinuria, or renal failure clues to microvascular disease

t.b: Is there retinal evidence of systemic disease? – Finds AV nicking, haemorrhages, exudates, papilloedema; if unavailable, use smartphone fundus adapters.
Is hypertension severe enough to cause retinopathy? – Systolic ≥180 mmHg or diastolic ≥120 mmHg supports malignant hypertension.
Is diabetes the driver of retinal changes? – Glucose ≥11 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) suggests uncontrolled diabetes.

t.a: Full blood count and malaria rapid test
t.b: Are retinal haemorrhages due to severe malaria? – Positive malaria test with anaemia supports the diagnosis.
Could opportunistic retinitis be present? – Positive HIV with CD4 <100 cells/µL raises suspicion for CMV retinitis.

sections.p: Recognise findings that demand urgent action.
b: Papilloedema – risk of herniation; treat raised ICP immediately
Grade IV hypertensive retinopathy – malignant hypertension, risk of stroke and renal failure
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy with vitreous haemorrhage – imminent vision loss

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then address ocular findings.
b: Malignant hypertension: IV labetalol or nicardipine (where available); avoid rapid over‑correction that can cause cerebral ischemia
Uncontrolled diabetes: insulin infusion or oral agents; avoid sulfonylureas if renal impairment present
Severe malaria: IV artesunate; avoid quinine if cardiac toxicity risk
CMV retinitis (HIV): oral valganciclovir; avoid ganciclovir if severe neutropenia
Papilloedema: raise head of bed, give IV mannitol or hypertonic saline; avoid steroids unless specific indication

sections.p: Regular retinal screening prevents irreversible damage.
b: Hypertensive patients: fundus exam every 1–2 years; tighter BP control reduces progression
Diabetics: annual dilated exam; earlier if glycaemic control poor
HIV patients: retinal exam at CD4 <200 cells/µL, repeat every 6 months
Optic neuritis – painful vision loss, no AV nicking
Retinal detachment – curtain‑like loss, no haemorrhages
Conjunctival injection – superficial redness, not retinal
Mild AV nicking can be age‑related, not pathological
Papilloedema may be absent early in raised ICP; rely on clinical signs too
Flame‑shaped haemorrhages can occur in anemia without hypertension

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of vision in one eye
Severe headache with vomiting and papilloedema

faq.q: Can I rely on a non‑dilated exam?
faq.a: Yes for screening; dilated exam improves detail for diabetic or proliferative disease.
Compression of a retinal vein at an arteriole crossing, indicating chronic hypertension.
It signals raised intracranial pressure that can cause brain herniation if untreated.

exam: A 35‑year‑old with malignant hypertension presents with blurred vision – what retinal findings confirm grade IV hypertensive retinopathy and what immediate step is required? — Look for papilloedema; start IV antihypertensive and assess for encephalopathy.

A diabetic patient’s fundus shows microaneurysms and hard exudates but no neovascularisation – how would you grade this and what follow‑up is indicated? — Moderate non‑proliferative diabetic retinopathy; arrange annual dilated exam and optimise glycaemic control.

A child with sickle cell disease has peripheral retinal neovascularisation – what is the likely stage and management? — Proliferative sickle‑cell retinopathy; refer for laser photocoagulation if available.

A patient with severe malaria has flame‑shaped haemorrhages on fundoscopy – what does this indicate and how does it affect treatment? — Retinal involvement suggests cerebral malaria; give IV artesunate and monitor neuro status.

You see papilloedema on fundoscopy in a patient with headache – what differential diagnoses must you consider and which investigation is priority? — Consider meningitis, TB meningitis, intracranial mass; obtain urgent CT scan or lumbar puncture if safe.

In an HIV‑positive patient with CD4 80 cells/µL, fundoscopy shows yellow‑white retinal lesions with haemorrhage – what is the diagnosis and first‑line therapy? — CMV retinitis; start oral valganciclovir, avoid ganciclovir if neutropenia.

A patient on chronic steroids presents with blurred vision; fundoscopy shows cotton‑wool spots – what systemic condition should you suspect? — Hypertensive retinopathy or diabetes; check blood pressure and glucose.
Why might a normal fundus not rule out raised intracranial pressure in early disease? — Papilloedema can lag behind ICP rise; rely on clinical signs and imaging.
